# Chap 6, Convergence Concepts


## Summary

The main topic of this chapter is to discuss the relationship between different kinds of convergence, so the graph below will be updated as we go deeper into the chapter. Further, many of the exercises are also about this topic, so we will summarize them here.


$$
\begin{array}{ccccc}
\text{Pointwise} & \xrightarrow{\text{Always}} & \text{Almost Sure (a.s.)} & \xrightarrow{\text{Always}} & \text{Probability (P)} \\
& \xleftarrow[\text{Example 6.1.1}]{\text{Fails}} & & \xleftarrow[\text{Example 6.2.1}]{\text{Fails}} &
\end{array}
$$


we can still recover a.s. convergence under extra conditions, such as:

- \(\{X_n\}\) is monotone (Ex 1),
- \(\Omega\) is discrete (Ex 17).

Also, if \(X_n \xrightarrow{P} X\), then every subsequence contains a further subsequence converging a.s. to \(X\).

Further, we get metrics that metrize convergence in probability on \(L^0\) modulo a.s. equality:

1. 
$$
d(X,Y)=E\left(\frac{|X-Y|^p}{1+|X-Y|^p}\right), \qquad p>0
$$
(Ex 12),

2.
$$
\rho(X,Y)=\inf\{\delta>0:\, P(|X-Y|\ge \delta)\le \delta\}
$$
(the Ky Fan metric, Ex 25).

By Theorem 6.3.1, every sequence that is Cauchy in probability converges in probability, so any metric generating convergence in probability is complete.


## Other Notes

### Alternative proof

#### Proposition 6.1.1 
In __Proposition 6.1.1__, the author explicitly construct an exception set for teaching propose, however we can do it in another way:

For any constant $c$, we have 
$$
P(M_n\leq c)=P(\max_{1\leq i\leq n}X_n\leq c)=\prod_{i=1}^nP(X_i\leq c)=F^n(c)\to0.
$$

What we want to prove is
$$
P(M_n\to\infty)=1
$$
Since $M_n$ is increasing with $n$, so $M_n\to\sup_n M_n$, therefore it is suffice to prove
$$
P(\sup_n M_n=\infty)=1
$$
or
$$
P(\sup_n M_n<\infty)=0
$$

Note that
$$
\{\sup_n M_n<\infty\}=\bigcup_{m\in\mathbb Z}\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty\{M_n\leq m\}
$$
and for any $m$,
$$
P(\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty\{M_n\leq m\})=\lim_{n\to\infty}P(M_n\leq m)=0
$$
so
$$
P(\bigcup_{m\in\mathbb Z}\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty\{M_n\leq m\})\leq\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}P(\bigcap_{n=1}^\infty\{M_n\leq m\})=0.
$$
Therefore $P(\sup_n M_n<\infty)=0$, that is
$$
M_n\to\infty\quad \text{a.s.}
$$

#### Theorem 6.2.1 (Convergence a.s. implies convergence i.p.)

Since $X_n\to X$ a.s., that is
$$
P(\{\omega:X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)\})=1
$$
and we can rewrite $\{\omega:X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)\}$ as
$$
\{\omega:X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)\}=\bigcap_{k=1}^\infty\bigcup_{N=1}^\infty\bigcap_{n=N}^\infty\{\omega:|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|\leq\frac1k\}
$$
so
$$
P(\bigcap_{k=1}^\infty\bigcup_{N=1}^\infty\bigcap_{n=N}^\infty\{\omega:|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|\leq\frac1k\})=1
$$
and
$$
P(\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty\bigcap_{N=1}^\infty\bigcup_{n=N}^\infty\{\omega:|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|>\frac1k\})=0,
$$
that is, for any $k\in\mathbb Z$, we have
$$
P(\bigcap_{N=1}^\infty\bigcup_{n=N}^\infty\{\omega:|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|>\frac1k\})=P(\limsup_n\{\omega:|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|>\frac1k\})=0,
$$
keep in mind that what we want is
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P(\{\omega:|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|>\frac1k\})=0,
$$
denote $A_n^{(k)}:=\{\omega:|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|>\frac1k\}=\{|X_n-X|>\frac1k\}$, for every $N$ and every $n\geq N$, we have
$$
A_n^{(k)}\subseteq\bigcup_{m\geq N}^\infty A_m^{(k)}
$$
so
$$
P(A_n^{(k)})\leq P(\bigcup_{m\geq N}^\infty A_m^{(k)})
$$
therefore
$$
\sup_{n\ge N} P(A_n^{(k)})\leq P(\bigcup_{m\geq N}^\infty A_m^{(k)})
$$
so
$$
\lim_{N\to\infty}\sup_{n\ge N} P(A_n^{(k)})\leq \lim_{N\to\infty}P(\bigcup_{m\geq N}^\infty A_m^{(k)})=P(\limsup_{m}\{|X_m-X|>\frac1k\})=0
$$
so we get
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P(\{\omega:|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|>\frac1k\})=0,
$$
since the probability of supreme of tail goes to $0$, then the probability of each term of tail should goes to $0$ as well.

For the last step, we still need it is true for any $\varepsilon>0$, not just $\frac1k$, we can select $k$ such that $\frac1k\leq\varepsilon$, so
$$
\{|X_n-X|>\varepsilon\}\subseteq\{|X_n-X|>\frac1k\},
$$
so we have for any $\varepsilon>0$
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P(\{|X_n-X|>\varepsilon\})\leq\lim_{n\to\infty}P(\{|X_n-X|>\frac1k\})=0.
$$

Thus $X_n\to X$ i.p. 

#### Theorem 6.6.1
Strictly speaking I did not provide another proof of this theorem, however, I reverse the order of proving in the book, so I still record my proof here.

##### (c) $\to$ (b)

What we have:

- $\{X_n\}$ is uniformly integrable;
- $X_n \xrightarrow{P} X$.

What we want:

\[
E|X_n-X_m| \to 0 \qquad (n,m\to\infty),
\]

that is, $\{X_n\}$ is $L_1$-Cauchy.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$, and define

\[
A_{n,m} := \{|X_n-X_m|>\varepsilon\}.
\]

Then

\[
\int |X_n-X_m|\,dP
=
\int_{A_{n,m}^c} |X_n-X_m|\,dP
+
\int_{A_{n,m}} |X_n-X_m|\,dP.
\]

On $A_{n,m}^c$, we have $|X_n-X_m|\le \varepsilon$, so

\[
\int_{A_{n,m}^c} |X_n-X_m|\,dP \le \varepsilon.
\]

Also, on $A_{n,m}$,

\[
|X_n-X_m|\le |X_n|+|X_m|,
\]

so

\[
\int_{A_{n,m}} |X_n-X_m|\,dP
\le
\int_{A_{n,m}} |X_n|\,dP + \int_{A_{n,m}} |X_m|\,dP.
\]

Hence

\[
\int |X_n-X_m|\,dP
\le
\varepsilon
+
\int_{A_{n,m}} |X_n|\,dP
+
\int_{A_{n,m}} |X_m|\,dP.
\]

Since $X_n \xrightarrow{P} X$, the sequence $\{X_n\}$ is Cauchy in probability, so

\[
P(A_{n,m}) = P(|X_n-X_m|>\varepsilon)\to 0
\qquad (n,m\to\infty).
\]

Since $\{X_n\}$ is uniformly integrable, by Theorem 6.5.1 it is uniformly absolutely continuous. Therefore, for the given $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta>0$ such that whenever $P(A)<\delta$,

\[
\sup_n \int_A |X_n|\,dP < \varepsilon.
\]

Thus, for $n,m$ large enough so that $P(A_{n,m})<\delta$, we have

\[
\int_{A_{n,m}} |X_n|\,dP < \varepsilon,
\qquad
\int_{A_{n,m}} |X_m|\,dP < \varepsilon.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\int |X_n-X_m|\,dP
<
\varepsilon+\varepsilon+\varepsilon
=
3\varepsilon
\]

for all sufficiently large $n,m$. Hence

\[
E|X_n-X_m| \to 0,
\]

so $\{X_n\}$ is $L_1$-Cauchy.

##### (a) $\to$ (c)

What we have:

\[
X_n \xrightarrow{L_1} X.
\]

What we want:

- $\{X_n\}$ is uniformly integrable;
- $X_n \xrightarrow{P} X$.

First, since $X_n \xrightarrow{L_1} X$, we have

\[
E|X_n-X| \to 0.
\]

So for every $\varepsilon>0$, Markov's inequality gives

\[
P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)
\le
\frac{1}{\varepsilon} E|X_n-X|
\to 0.
\]

Hence

\[
X_n \xrightarrow{P} X.
\]

Now we prove $\{X_n\}$ is uniformly integrable.

First, for every $n$,

\[
\int |X_n|\,dP
\le
\int |X_n-X|\,dP + \int |X|\,dP.
\]

Since $\int |X_n-X|\,dP \to 0$ and $X\in L_1$, it follows that

\[
\sup_n \int |X_n|\,dP < \infty.
\]

Next, we prove uniform absolute continuity.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Since $E|X_n-X|\to 0$, there exists $N_\varepsilon$ such that for all $n\ge N_\varepsilon$,

\[
\int |X_n-X|\,dP < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\]

Therefore, for any $A\in\mathcal{B}$ and any $n\ge N_\varepsilon$,

\[
\int_A |X_n|\,dP
\le
\int_A |X_n-X|\,dP + \int_A |X|\,dP
\le
\int |X_n-X|\,dP + \int_A |X|\,dP
<
\frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \int_A |X|\,dP.
\]

Since $X\in L_1$, the singleton family $\{X\}$ is uniformly integrable, so there exists $\delta_1>0$ such that

\[
P(A)<\delta_1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\int_A |X|\,dP < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\]

Hence, if $P(A)<\delta_1$, then for all $n\ge N_\varepsilon$,

\[
\int_A |X_n|\,dP < \varepsilon.
\]

So we have shown

\[
\sup_{n\ge N_\varepsilon}\int_A |X_n|\,dP < \varepsilon
\qquad \text{whenever } P(A)<\delta_1.
\]

Now consider the finite family

\[
\{|X_1|,\dots,|X_{N_\varepsilon-1}|\}.
\]

Since each $X_n\in L_1$ and the family is finite, it is uniformly integrable. Therefore, there exists $\delta_2>0$ such that

\[
P(A)<\delta_2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sup_{1\le n < N_\varepsilon}\int_A |X_n|\,dP < \varepsilon.
\]

Let

\[
\delta := \delta_1\wedge \delta_2.
\]

Then whenever $P(A)<\delta$, we have both

\[
\sup_{n\ge N_\varepsilon}\int_A |X_n|\,dP < \varepsilon
\]

and

\[
\sup_{1\le n < N_\varepsilon}\int_A |X_n|\,dP < \varepsilon.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sup_n \int_A |X_n|\,dP < \varepsilon
\qquad \text{whenever } P(A)<\delta.
\]

So $\{X_n\}$ is uniformly absolutely continuous. Together with

\[
\sup_n E|X_n|<\infty,
\]

Theorem 6.5.1 implies that $\{X_n\}$ is uniformly integrable.

Hence we have proved:

- $\{X_n\}$ is uniformly integrable;
- $X_n \xrightarrow{P} X$.

That is, (c) holds.

#### Theorem 6.6.2
##### (b) $\to$ (a)

Suppose $\{X_n\}$ is Cauchy in $L_p$. We want to show that there exists $X \in L_p$ such that

\[
\|X_n-X\|_p \to 0.
\]

Since $\{X_n\}$ is Cauchy in $L_p$, for each $j \ge 1$ there exists $N_j$ such that

\[
m,n \ge N_j
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\|X_n-X_m\|_p < 2^{-j}.
\]

Without loss of generality, take $N_1 < N_2 < \cdots$, and define

\[
n_j := N_j.
\]

Then $n_j \to \infty$, and since both $n_j$ and $n_{j+1}$ are at least $N_j$, we have

\[
\|X_{n_{j+1}}-X_{n_j}\|_p < 2^{-j}
\qquad (j \ge 1).
\]

Now define

\[
Y_K := \sum_{j=1}^K |X_{n_{j+1}}-X_{n_j}|,
\qquad
Y := \sum_{j=1}^\infty |X_{n_{j+1}}-X_{n_j}|.
\]

By Minkowski's inequality,

\[
\|Y_K\|_p
\le
\sum_{j=1}^K \|X_{n_{j+1}}-X_{n_j}\|_p
<
\sum_{j=1}^K 2^{-j}
\le 1.
\]

Hence

\[
E(Y_K^p)=\|Y_K\|_p^p \le 1.
\]

Since $Y_K \uparrow Y$, we also have $Y_K^p \uparrow Y^p$, so by the Monotone Convergence Theorem,

\[
E(Y^p)=\lim_{K\to\infty} E(Y_K^p)\le 1.
\]

Therefore $Y \in L_p$, and in particular $Y<\infty$ almost surely.

So for almost every $\omega$,

\[
\sum_{j=1}^\infty |X_{n_{j+1}}(\omega)-X_{n_j}(\omega)|<\infty.
\]

Hence the series

\[
\sum_{j=1}^\infty \bigl(X_{n_{j+1}}(\omega)-X_{n_j}(\omega)\bigr)
\]

converges absolutely, and therefore converges. Since its $K$th partial sum is

\[
\sum_{j=1}^K (X_{n_{j+1}}-X_{n_j}) = X_{n_{K+1}}-X_{n_1},
\]

it follows that $\{X_{n_j}\}$ converges almost surely. Define

\[
X := \lim_{j\to\infty} X_{n_j}
\qquad \text{a.e.}
\]

Next, for each $K$ we have

\[
X_{n_{K+1}}-X_{n_1}=\sum_{j=1}^K (X_{n_{j+1}}-X_{n_j}),
\]

so

\[
|X_{n_{K+1}}-X_{n_1}|
\le
\sum_{j=1}^K |X_{n_{j+1}}-X_{n_j}|
\le Y.
\]

Passing to the limit $K\to\infty$, we get

\[
|X-X_{n_1}| \le Y
\qquad \text{a.e.}
\]

Hence

\[
|X| \le |X_{n_1}| + Y.
\]

Since $X_{n_1} \in L_p$ and $Y \in L_p$, it follows that $X \in L_p$.

Now define the tails

\[
T_j := \sum_{k=j}^\infty |X_{n_{k+1}}-X_{n_k}|.
\]

Then $T_j \downarrow 0$ almost surely, and $0 \le T_j \le Y$. Also,

\[
|X-X_{n_j}| \le T_j
\qquad \text{a.e.}
\]

Therefore,

\[
|X-X_{n_j}|^p \le T_j^p \le Y^p.
\]

Since $Y^p \in L_1$ and $T_j^p \to 0$ almost surely, the Dominated Convergence Theorem gives

\[
E|X-X_{n_j}|^p \to 0.
\]

Thus

\[
\|X_{n_j}-X\|_p \to 0.
\]

Finally, we extend from the subsequence to the whole sequence. Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Since $X_{n_j}\to X$ in $L_p$, there exists $j$ such that

\[
\|X_{n_j}-X\|_p < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\]

Since $\{X_n\}$ is Cauchy in $L_p$, there exists $N$ such that

\[
m,n \ge N
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\|X_n-X_m\|_p < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\]

Choose $j$ large enough so that $n_j \ge N$. Then for every $n \ge N$,

\[
\|X_n-X\|_p
\le
\|X_n-X_{n_j}\|_p + \|X_{n_j}-X\|_p
<
\frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2}
=
\varepsilon.
\]

Hence

\[
\|X_n-X\|_p \to 0.
\]

So $\{X_n\}$ converges in $L_p$, and therefore $L_p$ is complete.



### Proof idea summarize

It is essentially impossible to recreate every proof in the book on my own, but I think it is still worthy summarizing the idea of proof using my own language.

#### Theorem 6.3.1(a)
We focus on the part that if $\{X_n\}$ is Cauchy in probability, then $\{X_n\}$ converges in probability.

When we only have "for any $\varepsilon,\delta>0$, there exists $n_0$ such that for all $r,s\geq n_0$, $P(|X_r-X_s|>\varepsilon)<\delta$", it is hard to get a convergent result from the void, therefore we need to get help from another space that is when Cauchy then convergent, i.e. a complete space, luckily, $\mathbb R$ is complete, so we can try to construct the required convergent result from $\{X_n(\omega)\}\subseteq\mathbb R$, however, __Example 6.2.1__ gave us a counter example such that convergence i.p. but not a.s., so we can not directly use something like $\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n$. So the idea is to construct a sub-sequence such that the probability that the difference of consecutive terms are large than some value is decreasing geometrically, that is
$$
P(|X_{n_{k+1}}-X_{n_k}|>2^{-k})\le 2^{-k}.
$$
then by Borel-Cantelli, we get a exception set that this sub-sequence is not Cauchy. That is, we construct a sub-seq is Cauchy a.s., and by the completeness of the real numbers, we construct a convergent result $X$, then by triangle inequality, the total sequence converges to our $X$ i.p.


#### Summary for Theorem 6.4.1

What we have is:

1. \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are iid.
2. \(F\) is strictly increasing at \(q:=F^{\leftarrow}(p)\), so for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
   \[
   F(q-\varepsilon)<p<F(q+\varepsilon).
   \]

What we want to show is:
\[
X^{(n)}_{[np]} \xrightarrow{P} F^{\leftarrow}(p).
\]

The idea is:

1. By the definition of convergence in probability, divide
   \[
   P\left(\left|X^{(n)}_{[np]}-q\right|>\varepsilon\right)
   \]
   into two tails:
   \[
   P\left(X^{(n)}_{[np]}>q+\varepsilon\right)
   \quad\text{and}\quad
   P\left(X^{(n)}_{[np]}<q-\varepsilon\right).
   \]

2. Translate both tails into events involving \(F_n\), because we know
   \[
   F_n(x)\xrightarrow{P}F(x).
   \]

3. Use both
   \[
   F_n(x)\xrightarrow{P}F(x)
   \quad\text{and}\quad
   \frac{[np]}{n}\to p,
   \]
   together with
   \[
   F(q-\varepsilon)<p<F(q+\varepsilon),
   \]
   to create a fixed positive gap, then bound each tail by a probability of the form
   \[
   P\bigl(|F_n(x)-F(x)|>\text{positive constant}\bigr)\to0.
   \]

Further, the reason that we need \(F\) is strictly increasing is because we need something that is locally unique to converge to.

X_n \xrightarrow{P} X
\]
then
\[
X_n \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} X.
\]

(b) Let $\{X_n\}$ be any sequence of random variables. Show that
\[
X_n \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} X
\]
iff
\[
\sup_{k \ge n} |X_k - X| \xrightarrow{P} 0.
\]

\medskip

(c) Points are chosen at random on the circumference of the unit circle. $Y_n$
is the length of the largest arc not containing any points when $n$ points
are chosen. Show $Y_n \to 0$ a.s.

\medskip

(d) Let $\{X_n\}$ be iid with common distribution $F(x)$ which satisfies
$F(x_0)=1$, $F(x)<1$ for $x<x_0$ with $x_0<\infty$. Prove
\[
\max\{X_1,\dots,X_n\} \uparrow x_0
\]
almost surely.

#### (a)

$\textbf{My idea:}$ Since $X_n\xrightarrow{P}X$, then there exists a sub-sequence $\{X_{n_k}\}$ such that
$X_{n_k}\xrightarrow{a.s.}X$, also, $\{X_n\}$ is monotone, so the limit in a.s. sense always exists, including $\pm\infty$, and all its convergent sub-sequences should have the same limit, so we have $X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}X$.

$\textbf{Answer:}$ Since $X_n\xrightarrow{P}X$, then there exists a sub-sequence $\{X_{n_k}\}$ such that
$X_{n_k}\xrightarrow{a.s.}X$, also, $\{X_n\}$ is monotone, so for any $\omega\in\Omega$ the limit always exists, including $\pm\infty$, denote $Y(\omega):=\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n(\omega)$, then we must have
$$
\lim_{k\to\infty}X_{n_k}=Y
$$
therefore $X=Y$ a.s., that is
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}X_n=X\quad\text{a.s.}
$$



$\textbf{Note:}$ Here we met the crucial difference between a.s. and pointwise, the monotoncity actually guarantees us convergent pointwise, but the subsequence we get is convergent a.s., therefore we cannot treat them as the same thing, so I modify __My idea__ a little.

#### (c)

$\textbf{My idea:}$ We can reconsider this question as: select $n-1$ points in a line with fixed length, and $Y_n$ be the longest part without any points, since for $n=1$, the arc is just the total line. Denote the length of the line as $L$, and each line as $X_n$,  so $X_n\leq L$, and $Y_n=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}X_n$, and $X_n$ are iid, so we can investigate the distribution function of $Y_n$
$$
P[Y_n\leq y]=P[X_1\leq y,\dots,X_n\leq y]=\prod_{i=1}^nP[X_i\leq y]=F_X^n(y).
$$
However, since $X_n$ are upper-bounded, so there exists $x_0$, such that $F(x_0)=1$, that is for $y\geq x_0$, we have $\sum_{n=1}^\infty F_X^n(y)=\infty$, by Borel-Cantelli, we have 
$$
P[\{Y_n\leq y\}\ \text{i.o.}]=0.
$$
$\textbf{Answer:}$ $\textbf{Answer:}$ Let the circumference of the circle be $L$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, choose $m$ such that
$$
\frac{L}{m}<\varepsilon,
$$
and divide the circle into $m$ equal subarcs $I_1,\dots,I_m$.

If $Y_n>\varepsilon$, then there exists an empty arc of length greater than $\varepsilon$. Such an arc must contain at least one of the subarcs $I_1,\dots,I_m$. Hence
$$
\{Y_n>\varepsilon\}\subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^m \{I_i \text{ contains no point}\}.
$$

For each fixed subarc $I_i$, the probability that one chosen point does not fall into it is
$$
1-\frac{L/m}{L}=1-\frac1m,
$$
so the probability that none of the $n$ chosen points falls into it is
$$
\left(1-\frac1m\right)^n.
$$
Therefore, by the union bound,
$$
P(Y_n>\varepsilon)
\le
\sum_{i=1}^m P(I_i \text{ contains no point})
=
m\left(1-\frac1m\right)^n \to 0.
$$
Thus
$$
Y_n\xrightarrow{P}0.
$$

Also, $Y_n$ is monotone decreasing, since adding a new point cannot make the longest empty arc longer. Hence by part (a),
$$
Y_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}0.
$$


$\textbf{Note:}$ These subarcs are not iid.






#### (d)

$\textbf{My idea:}$ Let $Y_n=\max\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}$, since $X_n$ are iid, for any $\varepsilon>0$, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(|Y_n-x_0|>\varepsilon)&=P(\{Y_n>\varepsilon+x_0\}\cup\{Y_n<x_0-\varepsilon\})\\
&\leq P(\{Y_n>\varepsilon+x_0\})+P(\{Y_n<x_0-\varepsilon\})\\
&=1-P(Y_n\leq x_0+\varepsilon)+\prod_{i=1}^nP(X_i<x_0-\varepsilon)\\
&=1-\prod_{i=1}^nP(X_i\leq x_0+\varepsilon)+\prod_{i=1}^nP(X_i<x_0-\varepsilon)\\
&=1-F^n(x_0+\varepsilon)+F^n((x_0-\varepsilon)-)\\
&\leq F^n(x_0-\varepsilon)\to0
\end{aligned}
$$
so $Y_n\xrightarrow{P}x_0$, and $Y_n$ is increasing with $n$, by (a), we have $Y_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}x_0$.

### Ex 12
::: problem
Let $\{X_n\}$ be a sequence of random variables.

\medskip

(a) If $X_n \xrightarrow{P} 0$, then for any $p>0$
\[

\]
and
\[
E\!\left(\frac{|X_n|^p}{1+|X_n|^p}\right)\to 0.
\tag{6.22}
\]

(b) If for some $p>0$ \((6.21)\) holds, then $X_n \xrightarrow{P} 0$.

(c) Suppose $p>0$. Show $X_n \xrightarrow{P} 0$ iff \((6.22)\).
:::

#### (a)

$\textbf{My idea:}$ Let 
$$
g(x)=\frac{|x|^p}{1+|x|^p},
$$
then $g(x)$ is continuous, by __corollary 6.3.1__, since $X_n\xrightarrow{P}0$, then $g(X_n)\xrightarrow{P}g(0)=0$, that is
$$
\frac{|X_n|^p}{1+|X_n|^p}\xrightarrow{P}0.
$$
Further, note that $\frac{|X_n|^p}{1+|X_n|^p}\leq1\in L_1$, by __Corollary 6.3.2__, we have

E\left(\frac{|X_n|^p}{1+|X_n|^p}\right)\to0.
$$

#### (b)

$\textbf{My idea:}$ Since $\frac{|X_n|^p}{1+|X_n|^p}\xrightarrow{P}0$, that is for any $\varepsilon>0$, we have
$$
P(\frac{|X_n|^p}{1+|X_n|^p}>\varepsilon)\to0,
$$
that is
$$
P(|X_n|^p>\varepsilon(1+|X_n|^p))\to0
$$
since $1+|X_n|^p\geq1$, then $\{|X_n|^p>\varepsilon\}\subseteq\{\frac{|X_n|^p}{1+|X_n|^p}>\varepsilon\}$, that is
$$
P(|X_n|^p>\varepsilon)\to0
$$
so
$$
P(|X_n|>\varepsilon^{\frac1p})\to0.
$$

$$
\{\frac{|X_n|^p}{1+|X_n|^p}>\frac{\varepsilon^p}{1+\varepsilon^p}\}=\{|X_n|^p>\varepsilon^p\}=\{|X_n|>\varepsilon\}
$$
so
$$
P(|X_n|>\varepsilon)\to0.
$$

$\textbf{Note:}$ The set relation  $\{|X_n|^p>\varepsilon\}\subseteq\{\frac{|X_n|^p}{1+|X_n|^p}>\varepsilon\}$ in __My idea__ is false.

#### (c)

$\textbf{My idea:}$ 
The "$\Rightarrow$" part is in (a)

"$\Leftarrow$"

By Markov Inequality, for any $\varepsilon>0$, we have
$$
P\left(\frac{|X_n|^p}{1+|X_n|^p}>\varepsilon\right)\leq\frac{E\left(\frac{|X_n|^p}{1+|X_n|^p}\right)}{\varepsilon}\to0
$$

so $\frac{|X_n|^p}{1+|X_n|^p}\xrightarrow{P}0$, by (b), we have $X_n\xrightarrow{P}0$.


$\textbf{Note:}$ In (c), __My idea__ is correct.

#### Summary
This exercise essentially gives a natural metric for convergence in probability. On $L^0$ modulo a.s. equality, for random variables $X,Y$, define
$$
d(X,Y)=E\left(\frac{|X-Y|^p}{1+|X-Y|^p}\right), \qquad p>0.
$$
This expectation always exists since
$$
0\le \frac{|X-Y|^p}{1+|X-Y|^p}\le 1 \in L^1.
$$

According to part (c), we have
$$
X_n\xrightarrow{P}X
\quad\text{iff}\quad
d(X_n,X)\to 0.
$$

So this exercise shows that convergence in probability is metrizable on $L^0$. In this sense, __Theorem 6.3.1__ can be viewed as a completeness statement for a metric generating convergence in probability.


### Ex 17
::: problem
In a discrete probability space, convergence in probability is equivalent to almost sure convergence.
:::

$\textbf{My idea:}$ Suppose $X_n\xrightarrow{P}X$, but $X_n\not\xrightarrow{a.s.}X$, then there exists $A\in\mathcal B$, $P(A)>0$ such that for $\omega\in A$, exists $\varepsilon_0>0$, for all $N>0$, exists $n_0\geq N$, such that
$$
|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|>\varepsilon_0.
$$
Since $\Omega$ is discrete, we always can pick an $\omega_0$ from $A$ such that $P(\omega_0)>0$, so for this $\omega_0$, there exists $\varepsilon_0>0$ for all $N>0$, we always have $n\geq N$ such that
$$
P(\{\omega_0:|X_n(\omega_0)-X(\omega_0)|>\varepsilon_0\})>0,
$$
that is, for $N=1$, there is $n_1$ such that $|X_{n_1}(\omega_0)-X(\omega_0)|>\varepsilon_0$, and for $N=n_1+1$, we also have $n_2$ such that $|X_{n_k}(\omega_0)-X(\omega_0)|>\varepsilon_0$, by doing so we explicitly construct a sub-sequence $X_{n_k}$, such that 
$$
P(\{\omega_0:|X_{n_k}(\omega_0)-X(\omega_0)|>\varepsilon_0\})>0
$$
then for this $\varepsilon_0$, it is contradict to 
$$
P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon_0)\to0
$$
so $X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}X$.

Conversely, we already have $X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}X\implies X_n\xrightarrow{P}X$.

$\textbf{Answer:}$

"$\Rightarrow$": It is a standard result that almost sure convergence implies convergence in probability in any probability space. Since $X_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} X$, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, $P(|X_n - X| > \varepsilon) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. Therefore, $X_n \xrightarrow{P} X$.

"$\Leftarrow$": Assume $X_n \xrightarrow{P} X$. We want to show $X_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} X$ in a discrete probability space $\Omega$. 

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that $X_n \not\xrightarrow{a.s.} X$. Let $A$ be the set of outcomes where convergence fails:
$$
A = \left\{\omega \in \Omega : \lim_{n \to \infty} X_n(\omega) \neq X(\omega)\right\}
$$
By our assumption that almost sure convergence fails, we have $P(A) > 0$.

Since $\Omega$ is a discrete probability space, any event is composed of a countable union of disjoint singleton events. Therefore:
$$
P(A) = \sum_{\omega \in A} P(\{\omega\})
$$
Because $P(A) > 0$, there must exist at least one specific outcome $\omega_0 \in A$ such that $P(\{\omega_0\}) = p_0 > 0$.

Since $\omega_0 \in A$, the deterministic sequence of real numbers $X_n(\omega_0)$ does not converge to $X(\omega_0)$. By the definition of non-convergence, there exists some $\varepsilon_0 > 0$ such that for any integer $N > 0$, there exists an $n \geq N$ satisfying:
$$
|X_n(\omega_0) - X(\omega_0)| \geq \varepsilon_0
$$
This allows us to explicitly construct a subsequence $n_k$ such that for all $k$:
$$
|X_{n_k}(\omega_0) - X(\omega_0)| \geq \varepsilon_0
$$
Now, consider the event $B_n = \{\omega \in \Omega : |X_n(\omega) - X(\omega)| \geq \varepsilon_0\}$. For every index in our subsequence $n_k$, the specific outcome $\omega_0$ is an element of $B_{n_k}$. By the monotonicity of probability measures, this implies:
$$
P(|X_{n_k} - X| \geq \varepsilon_0) \geq P(\{\omega_0\}) = p_0 > 0 \quad \text{for all } k
$$
Because there is a subsequence where the probability is bounded below by a strictly positive number $p_0$, the limit of the sequence of probabilities cannot be zero:
$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} P(|X_n - X| \geq \varepsilon_0) \neq 0
$$
This directly contradicts our initial assumption that $X_n \xrightarrow{P} X$. Therefore, our assumption that $X_n \not\xrightarrow{a.s.} X$ must be false, concluding that $X_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} X$.

$\textbf{Note:}$ __My idea__ is correct, and I provide the formalized answer here.


### Ex 19
::: problem
If $0 \le X_n \le Y_n$ and $Y_n \xrightarrow{P} 0$, check $X_n \xrightarrow{P} 0$.
:::

$\textbf{My idea:}$ Since $0\leq X_n\leq Y_n$, so for all $\varepsilon>0$, we have
$$
\{X_n>\varepsilon\}\subseteq\{Y_n>\varepsilon\},
$$
and since $Y_n\xrightarrow{P}0$, we have
$$
0\leq P(X_n>\varepsilon)\leq P(Y_n>\varepsilon)\to0,
$$
that is, $X_n\xrightarrow{P}0$.

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Assume $0 \leq X_n \leq Y_n$ and $Y_n \xrightarrow{P} 0$. We wish to show $X_n \xrightarrow{P} 0$.

Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be given. By the definition of convergence in probability, we must evaluate $\lim_{n \to \infty} P(|X_n - 0| > \varepsilon)$.

Since $0 \leq X_n \leq Y_n$, both $X_n$ and $Y_n$ are non-negative random variables. Therefore, $|X_n| = X_n$ and $|Y_n| = Y_n$. We can rewrite our target probability as $P(X_n > \varepsilon)$.

Consider the event $\{\omega \in \Omega : X_n(\omega) > \varepsilon\}$. Because $X_n(\omega) \leq Y_n(\omega)$ for all $\omega \in \Omega$, if $X_n(\omega) > \varepsilon$, it strictly follows that $Y_n(\omega) > \varepsilon$. This gives us the set inclusion:
$$
\{X_n > \varepsilon\} \subseteq \{Y_n > \varepsilon\}
$$
By the monotonicity property of probability measures, if $A \subseteq B$, then $P(A) \leq P(B)$. Applying this to our events yields:
$$
0 \leq P(X_n > \varepsilon) \leq P(Y_n > \varepsilon)
$$
We are given that $Y_n \xrightarrow{P} 0$, which means by definition $\lim_{n \to \infty} P(|Y_n| > \varepsilon) = 0$. Since $Y_n \geq 0$, this is equivalent to $\lim_{n \to \infty} P(Y_n > \varepsilon) = 0$.

Taking the limit as $n \to \infty$ of our inequality:
$$
0 \leq \lim_{n \to \infty} P(X_n > \varepsilon) \leq \lim_{n \to \infty} P(Y_n > \varepsilon) = 0
$$
By the squeeze theorem, $\lim_{n \to \infty} P(X_n > \varepsilon) = 0$. 

Therefore, $X_n \xrightarrow{P} 0$. 

$\textbf{Note:}$ __My idea__ is correct, and I provide the formalized answer here.


### Ex 21
::: problem
Recall the notation $d(A, B) = P(A \triangle B)$ for events $A, B$. Prove
$$d(A_n, A) \to 0 \text{ iff } 1_{A_n} \xrightarrow{L_2} 1_A.$$
:::

$\textbf{My idea:}$ For probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal B,P)$, and $A_n,A\in\mathcal B$, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
d(A_n,A)&=P(A_n\Delta A)\\
&=E(\mathbf1_{A_n\Delta A})\\
&=\int\mathbf1_{A_n\Delta A}dP\\
&=\int|\mathbf1_{A_n}-\mathbf1_{A}|dP\\
&=\int|\mathbf1_{A_n}-\mathbf1_{ A}|^2dP.\\
\end{aligned}
$$
therefore $d(A_n,A)\to0\Leftrightarrow \mathbf1_{A_n}\xrightarrow{L_2}\mathbf1_{ A}$.

$\textbf{Answer:}$
Let $d(A_n, A) = P(A_n \Delta A)$ and assume $d(A_n, A) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. We wish to determine the sense in which the sequence of indicator random variables $\mathbf{1}_{A_n}$ converges to $\mathbf{1}_A$.

First, observe the relationship between the indicator function of a symmetric difference and the difference of their respective indicator functions. For any $\omega \in \Omega$:
$$
\mathbf{1}_{A_n \Delta A}(\omega) = |\mathbf{1}_{A_n}(\omega) - \mathbf{1}_A(\omega)|
$$
This holds because the absolute difference is $1$ if and only if $\omega$ belongs to exactly one of the sets $A_n$ or $A$, which is the precise definition of the symmetric difference.

Furthermore, since the expression $|\mathbf{1}_{A_n}(\omega) - \mathbf{1}_A(\omega)|$ only takes values in the set $\{0, 1\}$, raising it to any power $p \geq 1$ leaves the value unchanged:
$$
|\mathbf{1}_{A_n} - \mathbf{1}_A|^p = |\mathbf{1}_{A_n} - \mathbf{1}_A| = \mathbf{1}_{A_n \Delta A}
$$
We can now evaluate the $L_p$ distance between the random variables:
$$
\begin{aligned}
E[|\mathbf{1}_{A_n} - \mathbf{1}_A|^p] &= E[\mathbf{1}_{A_n \Delta A}] \\
&= \int \mathbf{1}_{A_n \Delta A} dP \\
&= P(A_n \Delta A) \\
&= d(A_n, A)
\end{aligned}
$$
Since we are given that $d(A_n, A) \to 0$, it follows immediately that:
$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} E[|\mathbf{1}_{A_n} - \mathbf{1}_A|^p] = 0
$$
Therefore, the sequence of random variables $\mathbf{1}_{A_n}$ converges to $\mathbf{1}_A$ in $L_p$ for all $p \geq 1$ (including $L_1$ and $L_2$). 

Consequently, since convergence in $L_p$ implies convergence in probability, we also have $\mathbf{1}_{A_n} \xrightarrow{P} \mathbf{1}_A$. $\square$

$\textbf{Note:}$ __My idea__ is correct, and I provide the formalized answer here. Also, the formalized answer cover the $p>0$ situation.

Since $(X_n,Y_n)\xrightarrow{P}(X,Y)$, then for any $\varepsilon>0$, we should have
$$

$$
since $d$ is the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb R^2$, that is
$$

$$

$$
A_n^c\subseteq\{\omega:|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|^2\leq\varepsilon\}\cap\{\omega:|Y_n(\omega)-Y(\omega)|^2\leq\varepsilon\},
$$
taking complement in both sides, that is
$$
\{\omega:|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|^2>\varepsilon\}\cup\{\omega:|Y_n(\omega)-Y(\omega)|^2>\varepsilon\}\subseteq A_n.
$$
So
$$
\{\omega:|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|^2>\varepsilon\}\subseteq A_n
$$
and
$$
\{\omega:|Y_n(\omega)-Y(\omega)|^2>\varepsilon\}\subseteq A_n.
$$
Therefore we have
$$
0\leq P(|X_n-X|>\sqrt\varepsilon)\leq P(|X_n-X|^2+|Y_n-Y|^2>\varepsilon)\to0
$$
and 
$$
0\leq P(|Y_n-Y|>\sqrt\varepsilon)\leq P(|X_n-X|^2+|Y_n-Y|^2>\varepsilon)\to0.

and

$$
|X_n(\omega)-X(\omega)|^2+|Y_n(\omega)-Y(\omega)|^2\leq\varepsilon,
$$
so
$$
\{|X_n-X|\leq\sqrt\frac\varepsilon2\}\cap\{|Y_n-Y|\leq\sqrt\frac\varepsilon2\}\subseteq A_n^c,
$$
that is
$$
A_n\subseteq\{|X_n-X|>\sqrt\frac\varepsilon2\}\cup\{|Y_n-Y|>\sqrt\frac\varepsilon2\}
$$
so
$$
\begin{aligned}
0\leq P(|X_n-X|^2+|Y_n-Y|^2>\varepsilon)&\leq P(\{|X_n-X|>\sqrt\frac\varepsilon2\}\cup\{|Y_n-Y|>\sqrt\frac\varepsilon2\})\\
&\leq P(\{|X_n-X|>\sqrt\frac\varepsilon2\})+P(\{|Y_n-Y|>\sqrt\frac\varepsilon2\})\to0.

that is $(X_n,Y_n)\xrightarrow{P}(X,Y)$.

$$f(X_n, Y_n) \xrightarrow{P} f(X, Y).$$

$\textbf{Answer:}$ 

We will use Theorem 6.3.1, which tells us that for random variables $\{Z_n\}$, 
$Z_n \xrightarrow{P} Z$ if and only if for every subsequence $Z_{n_k}$ there exists a sub-subsequence $Z_{n_{k(i)}}$ such that $Z_{n_{k(i)}} \xrightarrow{a.s.} Z$.

Let $\{f(X_{n_k}, Y_{n_k})\}$ be any subsequence of $\{f(X_n, Y_n)\}$.

Since $(X_n, Y_n) \xrightarrow{P} (X, Y)$, then for the subsequence $(X_{n_k}, Y_{n_k})$, there exists a sub-subsequence $(X_{n_{k(i)}}, Y_{n_{k(i)}})$ such that:
$$
(X_{n_{k(i)}}, Y_{n_{k(i)}}) \xrightarrow{a.s.} (X, Y)
$$

That is, there exists $N \in \mathcal{B}$ with $P(N) = 0$, such that $\forall \omega \in N^c$:
$$
(X_{n_{k(i)}}(\omega), Y_{n_{k(i)}}(\omega)) \to (X(\omega), Y(\omega)) \quad \text{pointwise.}
$$

Further, $f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^d$ ($d \ge 1$) is continuous, so for $\omega \in N^c$:
$$
f(X_{n_{k(i)}}(\omega), Y_{n_{k(i)}}(\omega)) \to f(X(\omega), Y(\omega)) \quad \text{pointwise.}
$$

That is, 
$$
f(X_{n_{k(i)}}, Y_{n_{k(i)}}) \xrightarrow{a.s.} f(X, Y)
$$

By Theorem 6.3.1, we have:
$$
f(X_n, Y_n) \xrightarrow{P} f(X, Y)
$$
$\blacksquare$

So for each $k$, we have $P(|X-Y| \geq \frac{1}{k}) = 0$, therefore:
$$
0 \leq P\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^\infty \{|X-Y| \geq \frac{1}{k}\}\right) \leq \sum_{k=1}^\infty P(|X-Y| \geq \frac{1}{k}) = 0
$$
Hence $P(X \neq Y) = 0$.

"$\Leftarrow$" Since we have $P(X \neq Y) = 0$, so $\forall \delta > 0$, we have:
$$
P(|X-Y| \geq \delta) = 0 \leq \delta
$$
So $0$ is the infimum of $\{\delta > 0: P(|X-Y| \geq \delta) \leq \delta\}$, that is:
$$
\rho(X,Y) = 0
$$

Here we prove that $\rho$ is a metric.

1. The first part we have proven that $\rho(X,Y) = 0 \iff X=Y \text{ a.s.}$
2. Since $|X-Y| = |Y-X|$, we have $\rho(X,Y) = \rho(Y,X)$.
3. For r.v.s $X, Y, Z$, we want to show that:
$$
\rho(X,Y) \leq \rho(X,Z) + \rho(Z,Y)
$$
Select $\delta_1, \delta_2$ such that:
$$
P(|X-Z| \geq \delta_1) \leq \delta_1 \quad \text{and} \quad P(|Z-Y| \geq \delta_2) \leq \delta_2
$$
And we have:
$$
\{|X-Y| \geq \delta_1 + \delta_2\} \subseteq \{|X-Z| \geq \delta_1\} \cup \{|Z-Y| \geq \delta_2\}
$$
That is:
$$
P(|X-Y| \geq \delta_1 + \delta_2) \leq P(|X-Z| \geq \delta_1) + P(|Z-Y| \geq \delta_2) \leq \delta_1 + \delta_2
$$
so $\delta_1+\delta_2$ belongs to the admissible set for $\rho(X,Y)$, so we have
$$
\rho(X,Y) \leq \delta_1+\delta_2
$$
Taking the infimum on the right side, we have:
$$
\rho(X,Y) \leq \rho(X,Z) + \rho(Z,Y)
$$
$\blacksquare$

$\textbf{Note:}$ The method in proving triangle inequality is a standard routine to deal with infimum.

#### (b)

$\textbf{My idea:}$ 
$$
X_n \xrightarrow{P} X,
$$
that is, for all $\varepsilon>0$, we have
$$
P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\to 0.
$$

What we want to prove is
$$
\rho(X_n,X)\to 0.
$$

What we know is
$$
\rho(X_n,X)=\inf{\delta>0:P(|X_n-X|\ge \delta)\le \delta}.
$$

So for any $\delta>0$, select $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\varepsilon\le \delta$, so we have
$$
{|X_n-X|\ge \delta}\subseteq {|X_n-X|>\varepsilon}.
$$

Hence
$$
P(|X_n-X|\ge \delta)\le P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\to 0.
$$

Also,
$$
P(|X_n-X|\ge \delta)\le P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)<\delta.
$$

Therefore,
$$
\inf{\delta>0:P(|X_n-X|\ge \delta)<\delta}=0.
$$

For the converse, when we have
$$
\rho(X_n,X)\to 0,
$$
that is,
$$
\inf{\delta>0:P(|X_n-X|\ge \delta)\le \delta}\to 0,
$$
then for any $\varepsilon>0$,
$$
P(|X_n-X|\ge \varepsilon)\to 0.
$$
$\textbf{Answer:}$ 

"$\Rightarrow$" Assume $X_n \xrightarrow{P} X$. We want to show $\rho(X_n, X) \to 0$.
Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be given. 
By the definition of convergence in probability, we have:
$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} P(|X_n - X| \geq \varepsilon) = 0
$$
Thus, there exists an integer $N$ such that for all $n \geq N$:
$$
P(|X_n - X| \geq \varepsilon) \leq \varepsilon
$$
By the definition of $\rho$, the value $\varepsilon$ satisfies the condition in the set, meaning it is an upper bound for the infimum:
$$
\rho(X_n, X) = \inf\{\delta > 0 : P(|X_n - X| \geq \delta) \leq \delta\} \leq \varepsilon
$$
Since this holds for any $\varepsilon > 0$ for sufficiently large $n$, we have $\lim_{n \to \infty} \rho(X_n, X) = 0$.

"$\Leftarrow$" Assume $\rho(X_n, X) \to 0$. We want to show $X_n \xrightarrow{P} X$, which means for any $\varepsilon > 0$, $P(|X_n - X| \geq \varepsilon) \to 0$.
Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be given, and let $\eta$ be an arbitrary number such that $0 < \eta < \varepsilon$.
Since $\rho(X_n, X) \to 0$, there exists an $N$ such that for all $n \geq N$, $\rho(X_n, X) < \eta$.
Because the infimum is strictly less than $\eta$, there must exist some $\delta_n \in (0, \eta)$ such that:
$$
P(|X_n - X| \geq \delta_n) \leq \delta_n < \eta
$$
Since $\delta_n < \eta < \varepsilon$, we have the subset inclusion:
$$
\{|X_n - X| \geq \varepsilon\} \subseteq \{|X_n - X| \geq \delta_n\}
$$
Therefore, applying the probability measure:
$$
P(|X_n - X| \geq \varepsilon) \leq P(|X_n - X| \geq \delta_n) \leq \delta_n < \eta
$$
Since this holds for any arbitrary $\eta \in (0, \varepsilon)$ as $n \to \infty$, it must be that:
$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} P(|X_n - X| \geq \varepsilon) = 0
$$
Thus, $X_n \xrightarrow{P} X$.
$\blacksquare$

$\textbf{Note:}$ What we did here is actually purely use $\varepsilon-\delta$ language to show the limit is $0$.

#### (c)

$\textbf{My idea:}$ 

For Cauchy sequence \(\{X_n\}\), that is
\[
\forall \varepsilon>0,\ \exists N>0,\ \text{s.t.}\ \forall n,m\ge N,\ \text{we have}
\]
\[
\rho(X_n,X_m)<\varepsilon.
\]

What we need to show is that for this sequence, there exists \(X\), such that
\[
\rho(X_n,X)\to 0.
\]

By (b), we know that it is to show that there exists \(X\), such that
\[
X_n \xrightarrow{P} X.
\]

So what's left to be done is to show \(\{X_n\}\) is Cauchy in probability, since by Theorem 6.3.1, the limit exists.

And what we need is:
\[
\forall \eta>0,\qquad P(|X_n-X_m|\ge \eta)
\]
can be arbitrarily small.

So we can select \(\varepsilon\in(0,\eta)\), then for large \(n,m\), we have
\[
\rho(X_n,X_m)<\varepsilon,
\]
then we can select \(a_{n,m}\), such that \(a_{n,m}<\varepsilon\) and
\[
P(|X_n-X_m|\ge a_{n,m})\le a_{n,m}.
\]

Since \(\varepsilon<\eta\),
\[
P(|X_n-X_m|\ge \eta)\le P(|X_n-X_m|\ge a_{n,m})\le a_{n,m}\le \varepsilon.
\]

Since \(\varepsilon\) is arbitrary, we have that \(\{X_n\}\) is Cauchy in probability.

So the metric is complete.

$\textbf{Answer:}$ 
\[
\text{(c) For Cauchy sequence }\{X_n\}, \text{ that is } \forall \varepsilon>0,\ \exists N>0,\ \text{s.t. }\forall n,m>N,\ \text{we have}
\]
\[
\rho(X_n,X_m)<\varepsilon.
\]

What we need to show is that for this sequence, there exists \(X\), such that
\[
\rho(X_n,X)\to 0.
\]

By (b), we know that it is to show that there exists \(X\), such that
\[
X_n \xrightarrow{P} X.
\]

So what's left to be done is to show \(\{X_n\}\) is Cauchy in probability, since by Theorem 6.3.1, the limit exists.

And what we need is:
\[
\forall \eta,\gamma>0,\ \text{for large }n,m,\qquad P(|X_n-X_m|>\eta)<\gamma.
\]

So we can select
\[
\varepsilon\in(0,\min\{\eta,\gamma\}),
\]
then for large \(n,m\), we have
\[
\rho(X_n,X_m)<\varepsilon,
\]
then we can select \(a_{n,m}\), such that \(a_{n,m}<\varepsilon\) and
\[
P(|X_n-X_m|\ge a_{n,m})\le a_{n,m}.
\]

Since \(\varepsilon<\eta\),
\[
P(|X_n-X_m|\ge \eta)\le P(|X_n-X_m|\ge a_{n,m})\le a_{n,m}\le \varepsilon.
\]

Since \(\varepsilon\) is arbitrary, we have that \(\{X_n\}\) is Cauchy in probability.

So the metric is complete.

$\textbf{Note:}$ There are actually 2 things to control, so we need $\varepsilon\in(0,\min\{\eta,\gamma\})$

#### (d)

$\textbf{My idea:}$  Using __Example 6.2.1__ in page 170, or people call the typewritter sequence, we know that $X_n\xrightarrow{P}0$, but $X_n\not\xrightarrow{a.s.}0$, however, we can explicitly find a subsequence $X_1,X_4,X_7,...$ such that $X_{n_k}\xrightarrow{a.s.}0$. So if we can metrize almost sure convergence, for such $\{X_n\}$, all of its subsequences should not converge a.s..


$\textbf{Answer:}$  Suppose there exists a metric $d$ metrizing a.s. convergence.

Take the typewriter sequence $\{X_n\}$.

We know that
$$
X_n \xrightarrow{P} 0, \quad \text{but} \quad X_n \not\to 0 \ \text{a.s.}
$$

Since $X_n \xrightarrow{P} 0$, every subsequence $\{X_{n_k}\}$ has a further subsequence $\{X_{n_{k(i)}}\}$ such that
$$
X_{n_{k(i)}} \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} 0,
$$
that is,
$$
d(X_{n_{k(i)}},0)\to 0.
$$

And we should have
$$
X_n \not\to 0 \ \text{a.s.} \Rightarrow d(X_n,0)\not\to 0.
$$

By the property of metric spaces, a sequence $x_n$ converges to $x$ if and only if every subsequence has a further subsequence converging to $x$.

So we have
$$
d(X_n,0)\to 0,
$$
that is,
$$
X_n \xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} 0.
$$

This contradicts $X_n \not\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}} 0$. Therefore no such $d$ exists.

$\textbf{Note:}$ The knowledge we use here is that, a sequence $x_n$ converges to $x$ if and only if every subsequence has a further subsequence converging to $x$.

#### Summary

What we discussed in part (a) of this exercise is called the Ky Fan Metric, and we should note that we didn't use any fancy technique, all we used are juse $\varepsilon-N$ and the definition of infimum.

### Ex 2
::: problem
Let \(\{X_n\}\) be iid, \(EX_n=\mu\), \(\operatorname{Var}(X_n)=\sigma^2\). Set
\[
\bar X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i/n.
\]
Show
\[
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar X)^2 \xrightarrow{P} \sigma^2.
\]
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$ 

Let $\{X_i\}_{i\ge1}$ be iid with $E(X_1)=\mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X_1)=\sigma^2<\infty$.

Define
\[
Y_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar X_n)^2,
\quad \text{where} \quad
\bar X_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i.
\]

We want to show
\[
Y_n \xrightarrow{P} \sigma^2.
\]



* Step 1: Algebraic decomposition

We write
\[
Y_n
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2 - \bar X_n^2.
\]



* Step 2: Convergence of the first term

Let $Z_i = X_i^2$. Then $\{Z_i\}$ are iid and
\[
E|Z_1| = E(X_1^2) < \infty.
\]

By Khinchin’s Weak Law of Large Numbers (Chapter 7),
\[
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i
\xrightarrow{P} E(Z_1) = E(X_1^2).
\]


* Step 3: Convergence of the second term

By the Weak Law of Large Numbers (finite variance version),
\[
\bar X_n \xrightarrow{P} \mu.
\]

Since $x \mapsto x^2$ is continuous, by the Continuous Mapping Theorem,
\[
\bar X_n^2 \xrightarrow{P} \mu^2.
\]


* Step 4: Conclusion

Combining the two convergences,
\[
Y_n
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2 - \bar X_n^2
\xrightarrow{P}
E(X_1^2) - \mu^2.
\]

Since
\[
E(X_1^2) - \mu^2 = \operatorname{Var}(X_1) = \sigma^2,
\]

we conclude
\[
Y_n \xrightarrow{P} \sigma^2.
\]

$\textbf{Note:}$ This exercise requires the knowledge from chapter 7, which is the Khintchin's WLLN under the first moment hypothesis in page 205, if we don't use it, we still need to use the truncation method to by pass the $E(X_i^4)$ situation.

### Ex 4
::: problem
Let $\{X_n, n \ge 1\}$ be iid, $EX_n = 0, EX_n^2 = \sigma^2$. Let $a_n \in \mathbb{R}$ for $n \ge 1$. Set $S_n = \sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i$. Prove $\{S_n\}$ is $L_2$-convergent iff $\sum_{i=1}^\infty a_i^2 < \infty$.
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$ 

Let $S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i$, where $\{X_i\}$ are iid with $E(X_i)=0$, $\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2$.


($\Leftarrow$)

Assume $\sum_{i=1}^\infty a_i^2<\infty$.

For $n>m$,
\[
E(S_n-S_m)^2
=E\left(\sum_{i=m+1}^n a_i X_i\right)^2
=\sum_{i=m+1}^n a_i^2 E(X_i^2)
=\sigma^2\sum_{i=m+1}^n a_i^2.
\]

Thus $E(S_n-S_m)^2\to0$, so $\{S_n\}$ is Cauchy in $L_2$.  
Since $L_2$ is complete, $S_n$ converges in $L_2$.

---

($\Rightarrow$)

Assume $S_n$ converges in $L_2$. Then
\[
E(S_n-S_m)^2\to0.
\]

But
\[
E(S_n-S_m)^2=\sigma^2\sum_{i=m+1}^n a_i^2,
\]
so
\[
\sum_{i=m+1}^n a_i^2\to0.
\]

Thus $A_n=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2$ is Cauchy in $\mathbb{R}$, hence
\[
\sum_{i=1}^\infty a_i^2<\infty.
\]


### Ex 5
::: problem
Suppose $\{X_n\}$ is iid. Show $\{n^{-1}S_n, n \ge 1\}$ is ui provided $X_i \in L_1$.
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$ 


Let $S_n=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$, where $\{X_n\}$ are iid and $X_n\in L_1$.

We want to show $\left\{\frac{S_n}{n}\right\}$ is uniformly integrable.


Since $\{X_n\}\in L_1$ and iid, for each $X_i$, the integral $\int_A|X_i|dP$ absolutely continuous w.r.t. P, that is:
\[
\forall \varepsilon>0,\ \exists \delta>0,\ \text{if } A\in\mathcal{B} \text{ and } P(A)<\delta,
\text{ we have } \int_A |X_i|\,dP < \varepsilon/2.
\]

Then for $A\in\mathcal{B}$,
\[
\int_A \left|\frac{S_n}{n}\right| dP
=
\int_A \left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right| dP
\le
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \int_A |X_i| dP.
\]

Now decompose
\[
|X_i| = |X_i|1_{\{|X_i|\le K\}} + |X_i|1_{\{|X_i|>K\}}.
\]

Then
\[
\int_A |X_i| dP
=
\int_A |X_i|1_{\{|X_i|\le K\}} dP
+
\int_A |X_i|1_{\{|X_i|>K\}} dP.
\]

So
\[
\int_A \left|\frac{S_n}{n}\right| dP
\le
K P(A)
+
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \int |X_i|1_{\{|X_i|>K\}} dP.
\]

Since $\{X_i\}$ are iid,
\[
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n E\left(|X_i|1_{\{|X_i|>K\}}\right)
=
E\left(|X_1|1_{\{|X_1|>K\}}\right).
\]

Since $X_1\in L_1$, we can select $K$ large enough such that
\[
E\left(|X_1|1_{\{|X_1|>K\}}\right) < \varepsilon/2.
\]

Then for fixed $\varepsilon>0$, we can choose $\delta$ such that
\[
K P(A) < \varepsilon/2.
\]

Thus we have
\[
\sup_n \int_A \left|\frac{S_n}{n}\right| dP
\le
K P(A) + E\left(|X_1|1_{\{|X_1|>K\}}\right)
< \varepsilon.
\]

And for $A=\Omega$, we have
\[
\sup_n E\left|\frac{S_n}{n}\right|
\le
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n E|X_i|
=
E|X_1| < \infty.
\]

Hence $\left\{\frac{S_n}{n}\right\}$ is uniformly integrable.

$\textbf{Note:}$ 

At the early version of my idea, I wrote something like this:
\[
\sup_n \int_A \left|\frac{S_n}{n}\right| dP
\le
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \int_A |X_i| dP
=
\int_A |X_1| dP.
\]

To see what is going wrong here, we need to re-investigate the iid concept, which is not formally introduced in our book.

If $\{X_n\}$ are identically independently distributed (iid), firstly it means for every $n$,
\[
P\circ X_n^{-1}
\]
induces the same distribution function. Therefore we have
\[
E(X_n) = \int X_n dP = \int x F_n(dx) = \int x F_1(dx),
\]
and for any measurable function $g$,
\[
E(g(X_n)) = \int g(X_n) dP = \int g(x) F_n(dx) = \int g(x) F_1(dx).
\]

For the independent part, it means for $A_i \in \sigma(X_i)$, $A_i$ should be independent of $\sigma(X_j)$, $i\ne j$.

That means we cannot use the same $A\in\mathcal{B}$ to apply on each $X_i$ to get
\[
\int_A |X_i| dP.
\]

What we can do instead is to use truncation to control
\[
\int_A \left|\frac{S_n}{n}\right| dP.
\]

Since for fixed $K$,
\[
E\left(|X_i|1_{\{|X_i|>K\}}\right)
\]
are the same, and also
\[
E\left(|X_i|1_{\{|X_i|\le K\}}\right),
\]
we can control the integral.

So for
\[
\int_A |X_i| dP = E(|X_i|1_A),
\]
the issue is that $1_A$ is not a function of $X_i$.

### Ex 6
::: problem
Let $\{X_n\}$ be ui and let $X\in L_1$. Show $\{X_n-X\}$ is ui.
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Since $\{X_n\}$ is ui, we have
\[
\sup_n E|X_n|<\infty
\]
and for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta_1>0$ such that if $A\in\mathcal B$ and $P(A)<\delta_1$, then
\[
\sup_n\int_A |X_n|\,dP<\varepsilon/2.
\]

Since $X\in L_1$, there exists $\delta_2>0$ such that if $A\in\mathcal B$ and $P(A)<\delta_2$, then
\[
\int_A |X|\,dP<\varepsilon/2.
\]

Let $\delta=\min\{\delta_1,\delta_2\}$. Then for $A\in\mathcal B$, if $P(A)<\delta$, we have
\[
\sup_n\int_A |X_n-X|\,dP
\le
\sup_n\int_A |X_n|\,dP+\int_A |X|\,dP
<
\varepsilon.
\]

Further,
\[
\sup_n E|X_n-X|
\le
\sup_n E|X_n|+E|X|<\infty.
\]

Hence $\{X_n-X\}$ is ui.

$\textbf{Note:}$ I get passed at my first try.


### Ex 8
::: problem
Suppose $\{X_n\}$ and $\{Y_n\}$ are ui in the same probability space. Show $\{X_n+Y_n\}$ is ui.
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

Since $\{X_n\}$ and $\{Y_n\}$ are ui, for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\delta_1(\varepsilon)>0$, such that for $A\in\mathcal{B}$, if $P(A)<\delta_1$, then
\[
\sup_n \int_A |X_n|\,dP < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\]

And there exists $\delta_2(\varepsilon)>0$, such that for $A\in\mathcal{B}$, if $P(A)<\delta_2$, then
\[
\sup_n \int_A |Y_n|\,dP < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\]

Let
\[
\delta=\min\{\delta_1,\delta_2\}.
\]

Then for $A\in\mathcal{B}$, if $P(A)<\delta$, we have
\[
\sup_n \int_A |X_n+Y_n|\,dP
\le
\sup_n\left(
\int_A |X_n|\,dP+\int_A |Y_n|\,dP
\right)
\]
\[
\le
\sup_n\int_A |X_n|\,dP
+
\sup_n\int_A |Y_n|\,dP
<
\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
=
\varepsilon.
\]

And
\[
\sup_n E|X_n+Y_n|
\le
\sup_n E|X_n|+\sup_n E|Y_n|
<\infty.
\]

So $\{X_n+Y_n\}$ is ui.

### Ex 3
::: problem
Suppose $X\ge 0$, $Y\ge 0$, and $p\ge 0$.

(a) Prove
\[
E((X+Y)^p)\le 2^p\{E(X^p)+E(Y^p)\}.
\]

(b) If $p>1$, replace $2^p$ by $2^{p-1}$.

(c) If $0\le p\le 1$, replace $2^p$ by $1$.
:::

$\textbf{Answer:}$

#### (a)

Since
\[
X+Y\le 2\max(X,Y),
\]
we have
\[
(X+Y)^p\le (2\max(X,Y))^p
=2^p(\max(X,Y))^p.
\]

Also,
\[
(\max(X,Y))^p\le X^p+Y^p.
\]

Therefore,
\[
(X+Y)^p\le 2^p(X^p+Y^p).
\]

Taking expectation on both sides,
\[
E((X+Y)^p)\le 2^p\{E(X^p)+E(Y^p)\}.
\]

#### (b)

Let $f(x)=x^p$, $x\ge0$. When $p>1$, $f$ is convex.

By Jensen's inequality,
\[
\left(\frac X2+\frac Y2\right)^p
\le
\frac12X^p+\frac12Y^p.
\]

Thus
\[
\left(\frac{X+Y}{2}\right)^p
\le
\frac12(X^p+Y^p),
\]
so
\[
(X+Y)^p
\le
2^{p-1}(X^p+Y^p).
\]

Taking expectation,
\[
E((X+Y)^p)
\le
2^{p-1}\{E(X^p)+E(Y^p)\}.
\]

#### (c)

When $X(\omega)+Y(\omega)=0$, both sides are $0$, so the inequality holds.

When $X(\omega)+Y(\omega)>0$, we have
\[
0\le \frac{X}{X+Y}\le 1,
\qquad
0\le \frac{Y}{X+Y}\le 1.
\]

Since $0\le p\le 1$, for $0\le t\le 1$,
\[
t^p\ge t.
\]

So
\[
\left(\frac{X}{X+Y}\right)^p
+
\left(\frac{Y}{X+Y}\right)^p
\ge
\frac{X}{X+Y}
+
\frac{Y}{X+Y}
=
1.
\]

Multiplying by $(X+Y)^p$, we get
\[
X^p+Y^p\ge (X+Y)^p.
\]

Therefore,
\[
(X+Y)^p\le X^p+Y^p.
\]

Taking expectation,
\[
E((X+Y)^p)\le E(X^p)+E(Y^p).
\]
